title: Marketing Attribution Guide: How to Choose the Right Marketing & SEO Platform
description: Practical marketing attribution guidance with planning steps, evaluation criteria, risks, and implementation checks.
author: Emily Nakamura

sections.title: Define the question attribution should answer
sections.body: Attribution can describe how recorded touchpoints relate to conversions, but it does not automatically prove that a channel caused a sale. Decide whether the immediate need is campaign reporting, budget allocation, lead-source tracking, or causal measurement. Define the conversion, time window, channel taxonomy, and business unit before choosing a model. If teams disagree on what counts as a conversion, fix that first.

sections.title: Map the customer journey and data gaps
sections.body: Trace the journey from first interaction through forms, CRM, sales conversations, purchase, and retention. Identify where identifiers are lost, consent prevents collection, offline activity is not recorded, or multiple systems overwrite source values. Document the limits of each source and avoid treating missing data as evidence that a channel had no influence. Make the data flow and ownership visible to both marketing and analytics.

sections.title: Choose an attribution model deliberately
sections.body: Last-click is easy to explain but overweights the final recorded touch. First-click highlights discovery but ignores later influence. Position-based or time-decay models encode assumptions that should be stated explicitly. Data-driven models require sufficient reliable data and still depend on measurement choices. Compare model outputs on the same period and explain how the model changes budget decisions rather than presenting one model as universally correct.

sections.title: Standardize campaign tracking
sections.body: Create a naming convention for source, medium, campaign, content, and term. Validate links before launch and preserve parameters through redirects and forms. Test cross-domain journeys, email clicks, paid campaigns, QR codes, and partner referrals. Establish a process to correct mis-tagged traffic without silently rewriting history. Keep campaign names human-readable and stable enough for reports to remain useful after a team member leaves.

sections.title: Respect consent and privacy
sections.body: Inventory analytics tags, cookies, SDKs, and server-side events. Verify which tags fire before and after consent and how withdrawal changes behavior. Minimize identifiers, restrict access, and set retention periods that fit the purpose. Confirm requirements for the relevant jurisdictions with qualified privacy or legal advice; attribution requirements do not override data-protection obligations.

sections.title: Validate against business outcomes
sections.body: Reconcile conversions and revenue with an authoritative CRM, billing, or finance source. Check duplicate events, refunds, delayed conversions, cross-device gaps, and changes in consent rates. Compare model output with a controlled experiment when you need to estimate incremental impact. A channel that receives credit in a model is not necessarily a channel that caused the result.

sections.title: Measure operational quality
sections.body: Track the percentage of campaigns using valid tags, missing-source rate, duplicate conversion rate, event delay, and differences between analytics and the system of record. Assign owners for taxonomy, tracking implementation, data quality, and model changes. Keep a change log so that a tracking release does not create an unexplained break in historical reports.

sections.title: Decision checklist
sections.body: Choose a setup that makes assumptions explicit, preserves data quality, respects consent, and can be reconciled with business records. Document the model, known blind spots, and conditions for reassessment. Use attribution for consistent reporting and combine it with experiments or other evidence when making causal budget decisions.
